Affiliation * 1 Laboratory of Inorganic and Analytical Chemistry, Helsinki University of Technology, Espoo, Finland. * PMID: 9297986 * DOI: 10.1007/978-1-4612-1964-4_3 Abstract EDTA can be extremely persistent in WWTP and also in natural waters; DTPA seems more biodegradable. However, the biodegradability of DTPA might be of negligible significance as EDTA, and in some cases also DTPA, are generally found in the receiving waters of many industrial areas, thus being classified as one of the major organic pollutants discharged in waters. The photochemical degradation of Fe(III) complexes of these compounds is documented, but the extent to which these results can be applied to natural waters is not clear. There exist still some uncertainties in the chemical speciation, adsorption, overall degradation, and ultimately the eutrophication effect of EDTA and especially of DTPA. It can be inferred that EDTA can affect the essential and nonessential metal balance in natural waters as well as in aquatic organisms, even in the long term. The estimation of the chemical speciation of EDTA and DTPA in natural waters is a challenging task because of of the complexicity of the system and should be based not only on equilibrium calculations but also on direct analytical determinations of diverse metal species. Unfortunately, analytical methods for speciation studies at environmentally relevant concentrations are not available. Also, monitoring of EDTA or DTPA in sediments and solid particles has not been initiated. EDTA and DTPA are not expected to be acutely toxic to aquatic organisms. On the other hand, in natural waters, several compounds affect organisms simultaneously. Therefore, EDTA and DTPA can contribute to the aquatic toxicity at significantly lower concentration than those determined by short-term toxicity tests. Also, more studies should be directed to estimating chronic effects, including the possible imbalance of body calcium in animals and other organisms. EDTA and DTPA can certainly desorb heavy metals bound to sediments and also prevent heavy metal sedimentation, thus increasing their cycle in water. However, these metal complexes are not expected to be as bioavailable as a free metal ions. Taken together, EDTA and DTPA, being persistent compounds, contribute to the general chemicalization of the aquatic environment. They can also cause several indirect and, under extreme circumstances, direct effects in the aquatic environment. Thus, their release into natural waters should be minimized wherever possible. fetched_contents.text: Redox property of coordinated iron ion enables activation of O2 via in-situ generated H2O2 and additionally added H2O2 in EDTA-chelated Fenton reaction Introduction Since the Fenton reaction was reported a century ago, the typical technique was thoroughly investigated and extensively employed in different domains of water purification (Yang et al., 2013), protein modification (Xu and Chance, 2007), material preparation (Feng et al., 2016), molecular synthesis (Chen and White, 2007), and tumor therapy (Tang et al., 2019). Well known as a hydroxyl radical (•OH) production process. Fenton system was traditionally deemed to be dominated by the activation of hydroxyl peroxide (H2O2) by ferrous ions (Fe2+) and subsequent interaction between in-situ generated •OH and targeted substrates, owing to the high redox potential of •OH and its strong ability to snatch an electron from the substrates (Zeng et al., 2020). However, in addition to the main reaction, Fe2+ could also initiate the side reactions among the Fe2+/Fe3+ pair, H2O2, various intermediate radicals, and dissolved oxygen, which has been overlooked and hardly addressed in the literature. Substantially, Fenton system was a generation system of several reactive oxygen species (•OH; superoxide radical, O2•−; singlet oxygen; 1O2) via the chain-reactions (Table 1, reaction 1–7), which employed H2O2 and O2 as radical precursors and Fe2+/Fe3+ as electron-donor or electron-acceptor for triggering or terminating the generation of radicals (Zeng et al., 2022). In most of the literatures, the “side reactions” among the radicals and other substrates were always overlooked, and few researchers targeted to tuning the electron flow in the chain-reactions. By tuning the composition/parameters in the system, the chain reactions can be readily oriented to different ‘radical configurations’ (Li et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2022). For instance, the Fe2+/H2O2 pair with a moderate ratio could efficiently produce •OH, while excess Fe2+ ions can terminate •OH and lower the •OH concentration in the system; the Fe3+/H2O2 pair could produce •OH and O2•−, but the rate was highly impeded by the slow O2•− formation from H2O2 with the Fe3+conversion to Fe2+ (reaction 2) (Chen et al., 2011). Several types of research explored to introduce reductants into the system for accelerating the Fe2+ regeneration, steering the electron flow toward a designed route (reductants→Fe3+/Fe2+→H2O2) for continuously yielding •OH. Inevitably, the •OH could be scavenged by excess reductants, thereby the reductant concentration should be well-controlled at low dosage mode with high frequency (Li et al., 2020). In the system, the reductants acted as the actual electron donor of the modified Fenton system. In a recent study, the metallic molybdenum as co-catalyst enhanced the O2•− conversion to singlet oxygen (1O2) in Fenton system, thereby inducing the co-existence of 1O2 and •OH for organic decontamination or disinfection (Yi et al., 2019). It has been reported that the complexation of iron ions with chelating agents could change the redox potential of the Fe3+/Fe2+ pair (Yang et al., 2020a), further improving the activity of iron with dissolved oxygen for producing reactive oxygen species (ROS). Using tripolyphosphate as a ligand, Fe2+ could convert oxygen to O2•− rapidly, while a similar reaction occurred to free Fe2+ at a negligible rate (Reaction 8) (Zhang et al., 2022). In natural environment, hydroxyl radical (•OH) production by electron transfer from ferrous-bearing clay minerals to oxygen in Fe2+ and natural organic matter (NOM) like humic acid (HA) coexisting systems have been increasingly discovered. The electron selectivity can be regulated by changing the ratio of ferrous to HA, converting the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) from one- to two-electron transfer process with H2O2 as the main intermediate, and enhance the yield of •OH production (Xie et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2023, 2021). Ethylene diamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) was commonly used in chemical industry process, like the metallochromic indicator, or low-cost and easily available additive to beauty products. Fenton reaction coupled with EDTA as a novel Fenton-like system was frequently reported in groundwater treatment and soil remediation and it indeed upgrade the decontamination capacity (Rastogi et al., 2009). Furthermore, coupling chelating agents with Fenton process could also be an alternative option to stabilize Fe2+/Fe3+ at basic conditions, owing to the ligands complex with metal ions strongly (De Laat et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2018). The ability of the reactive species in EDTA-Fenton system has not been explored entirely and its generation mechanism still remain to be unveiled. In these processes, the traditional Fenton chain reactions are able to be regulated by coupling the ligand to promote various promising reactive species. Also, the influence of oxygen as the most essential component in air on chelating Fenton system may have been overlooked. Recently, some studies investigated in Fe2+/TPP/O2 system, the production of radicals is a Fe2+/TPP molar ratio dependent process. The amounts of electrons accepted by oxygen as an electron acceptor varies depending on the ratio of ferrous to ligand. When [Fe2+]0 ≥ [TPP]0, the O2•− in the system was rapidly converted to •OH and the pollutants were degraded mainly by oxidation. Comparing to [Fe2+]0 < [TPP]0, the O2•− in the system accumulated, and the pollutants could be degraded by reduction to some refractory compounds (Zhang et al., 2022, 2019). In the meantime, Some researches also attempted to induce the yield of high valent iron Fe(IV) under neutral conditions in Fenton combining with ligands. Unluckily, owing to the strong steric hindrance by some impeded the interaction between hydrogen peroxide and iron ligand complexes, leading to the transformation of non-radical process become radical process. fetched_contents.text: hEDTA and EDDS as sustainable and harmless alternatives to NTA as trace metal chelators in Methanothermobacter marburgensis cultivation Abstract The thermophilic methanogenic archaea Methanothermobacter spp. are applied as archaeal cell factories in industrial processes for methane production. Recently, secretion of commodity chemicals by M. marburgensis, such as amino acids, organic acids, or lipids has been observed. Together with the genetic tools available, genetically engineered cell factories for commodity chemical production from CO2 can be developed. However, the toxicity of the commonly used trace metal chelator Nitrilotriacetic acid (NTA) for M. marburgensis blocks potential regulatory approval for human applications. Therefore, we identified EDDS and hEDTA as suitable non-toxic alternatives as metal chelators for M. marburgensis. While EDDS reduces the specific growth rate (µ) of M. marburgensis by 40%, hEDTA shows the same µ as with NTA usage. Additionally, hEDTA offers cost wise a sustainable economic alternative to NTA with 23 € m− 3 of growth medium compared to 13 € m− 3 with NTA. With hEDTA as a harmless alternative to NTA, we are one step closer to industrial sustainable commodity chemical production from CO2 with M. marburgensis. Keywords: Microbiology, Biotechnology, Archaea, Methanogens Introduction Chelating agents are versatile substances that are widely utilized in analytic, scientific, industrial, or medical applications due to their ability to form stable complexes with metal ions. In medicine, chelators play a crucial role in the treatment of heavy metal poisoning by binding toxic metals such as lead, mercury, and arsenic, to facilitate their safe excretion from the human body (Crichton et al. 2016). Furthermore, chelating agents are commonly used for analytical metal detection and quantification in drinking water, soil remediation, and removal of heavy metals from wastewater streams (Byegård et al. 1999; Kociałkowski et al. 1999; Nyamato 2023; Xing et al. 2019). The food industry employs chelators to prevent metal-catalyzed oxidation, thereby enhancing product stability and shelf life (Ogiwara et al. 2016). Additionally, chelators are an integral part of industrial processes such as textile manufacturing and paper production (Goto et al. 2023). In agriculture, chelating agents improve trace metal availability in plants, ensuring efficient uptake of those essential minerals. As a side effect in plant treatment with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) as chelator, it has been demonstrated that the bioavailability of trace metals is then reduced for soil microorganisms (Kaurin et al. 2020; Lee and Sung 2014). This reduced bioavailability has also been applied to Escherichia coli cultivation, where trace zinc starvation was introduced through addition of EDTA to the minimal medium due to its high binding affinity of zinc to reduce its bioavailability and activate specific biosynthetic pathways for putative biotechnological application (Paterson et al. 2023). Similarly, EDTA has also been shown to inhibit growth of methanogenic archaea in anaerobic digesters (Pham 2017; Vintiloiu et al. 2013). On the other hand, chelating agents can also have beneficial effects on the bioavailability of trace metals (Thanh et al. 2016). Those chelating agents are commonly used in cultivation of microorganisms which are dependent on high abundance of heavy metals, such as acetogenic bacteria or methanogenic archaea (Abdel Azim et al. 2017; Choong et al. 2016). Especially methanogenic archaea have a need for relatively high concentrations of iron, nickel, or cobalt due to their unique set of enzymes that enable growth on molecular hydrogen (H2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) (Lyu et al. 2018). Commonly, nitrilotriacetic acid (NTA) is used as a chelating agent for pure cultures of methanogenic archaea (Zeikus and Wolfe 1972). The growing interest in industrial applications of methanogenic archaea as cell factories for human-applied commodity chemicals from CO2, however, makes the use of NTA for regulatory approval nearly impossible due to its toxic and carcinogenic characteristics (Hartwig 2022). Alternatives to NTA, such as EDTA, ethylenediaminedisuccinic acid (EDDS), hydroxyethylethylenediaminetriacetic acid (hEDTA), or citric acid have been successfully proven to act as harmless chelating agents for fermentation in mixed cultures (Fabbricino et al. 2013; Lanigan et al. 2002; Li et al. 2023; Thanh, Ketheesan, Yan, et al., 2017; Zhang et al. 2021). For the model microorganism in methanogenic archaea, Methanothermobacter marburgensis, which is already applied in large scale industrial processes for methane production in power to gas systems (Götz et al. 2016), an alternative to NTA has not been implemented before to our knowledge. M. marburgensis is an aquatic thermophilic methanogenic archaeon isolated from anaerobic sewage sludge in Germany with an optimal growth temperature at 65 °C. Due to its robust cell-wall characteristics and planktonic growth behavior it is highly robust and resilient to shear forces which facilitate bioreactor fermentation (Bernacchi et al. 2014; Seifert et al. 2014). Besides its use as cell factory for methane production, it has been observed that M. marburgensis naturally secretes amino acids (Reischl et al. 2025; Taubner et al. 2023). Additionally, with the recently established tools for genetic engineering, it has already been proven that synthetic biosynthesis pathways can be integrated into the genome of M. marburgensis to alter the secretion pattern of amino acids (Klein et al. 2025). This marks the first step towards commodity chemical production with M. marburgensis and urges the need for a sustainable alternative to NTA as trace metal chelator. Mechanistic limitations of EDTA in Fenton-based remediation

EDTA can improve Fenton reactivity by altering the redox behavior of Fe3+/Fe2+ and influencing radical generation, but this effect is conditional and often accompanied by tradeoffs. The EDTA-chelated Fenton reaction is described as a system in which coordinated iron enables activation of O2 via in-situ generated H2O2 and additionally added H2O2, which suggests that EDTA can change the redox environment and promote radical production [N2-F2]. At the same time, the literature emphasizes that Fenton systems are not just about •OH; they are broader systems that generate multiple reactive oxygen species, including O2•− and possibly singlet oxygen, and that these species are produced through chain reactions involving Fe2+/Fe3+ and H2O2 [N2-F2]. EDTA therefore does not simply increase •OH yield; it can shift the overall radical configuration and the balance between different ROS species [N2-F2].

One key limitation is that EDTA can enhance Fe2+ generation from H2O2 and thus affect the Fe2+/Fe3+ speciation that drives the system. The evidence notes that Fe2+ could also initiate side reactions among Fe2+/Fe3+, H2O2, various intermediate radicals, and dissolved oxygen, and that these side reactions have been largely overlooked [N2-F2]. This implies that EDTA may complicate rather than simplify the Fenton mechanism by introducing additional reactivity pathways, some of which may compete with the target remediation reaction or reduce overall efficiency. The same source also says that excess Fe2+ can terminate •OH and lower its concentration in the system, while Fe3+/H2O2 can produce •OH and O2•− but at a rate impeded by slow O2•− formation from H2O2 via Fe3+ conversion to Fe2+ [N2-F2]. This shows that EDTA may not always increase radical yield in a straightforward way; it can instead shift the system toward different radical configurations, which may be less favorable for the intended oxidation process [N2-F2].

Soil organic matter is another major mechanistic limitation. The Fenton reaction is affected by soil organic matter (SOM), and the evidence states that SOM can sometimes act in a dual way, either promoting or inhibiting the reaction, with the effects being sometimes conflicting [N3-F3]. The cited review explicitly says that the effects of SOM on Fenton reaction are reported either promoting or inhibiting and sometimes both, and that the most studied and effective parameters for evaluating SOM’s impact are initial reagents and pH [N3-F3]. In the broader context of EDTA-enhanced Fenton, this means that SOM can interfere with reactivity by scavenging radicals, changing the delivery of H2O2 or Fe2+/Fe3+, or altering the microenvironment in a way that suppresses efficiency [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that pH change, H2O2 scavenging via non-productive reactions, and delivery of H2O2, Fe2+, acid, and other factors can limit the reaction [N3-R1]. This is important because EDTA is often used to stabilize Fe2+/Fe3+ in basic conditions, but the same stabilization can be undermined by pH sensitivity [N3-R3].

The evidence also highlights pH sensitivity as a central constraint. The Fenton process requires acidification and subsequent neutralization, and the pH range is a major disadvantage of the process [N3-R3]. The same source reports that EDTA and other iron sources were studied in the photo-Fenton process at natural pH to remove micropollutants, suggesting that pH is a critical variable for both conventional and EDTA-enhanced systems [N3-R2]. This means that EDTA-based Fenton remediation is not inherently robust to pH fluctuations; rather, it depends on careful control of the operating pH. The review on soil organic matter further emphasizes that pH affects SOM and that SOM effects on Fenton reaction can be studied in relation to pH [N3-F3]. Overall, pH sensitivity implies that EDTA can improve reactivity under optimized conditions, but it may also make the system vulnerable to pH shifts in the field, where natural variation is common [N3-R3][N3-F3].

Finally, the speciation effects on Fe2+/Fe3+ and radical yield are central. EDTA can change the redox potential of the Fe3+/Fe2+ pair, which improves the activity of iron with dissolved oxygen for producing reactive oxygen species [N2-F2]. However, this speciation effect can also create dependence on ligand-metal interactions. The evidence notes that EDTA is commonly used in chemical processes and as an additive, but it also says that the ability of reactive species in EDTA-Fenton systems has not been fully explored and its generation mechanism still remains to be unveiled [N2-F2]. In other words, EDTA can create a more favorable speciation environment for radicals, but the exact mechanism and the resulting radical yield are not fully understood. The mechanistic complexity is further compounded by the fact that ligands can influence oxygen as an electron acceptor and that the ratio of Fe2+ to ligand can determine whether O2•− is rapidly converted to •OH or accumulates [N2-F2]. This indicates that EDTA may improve speciation-dependent radical yield, but only within a narrow set of conditions that are sensitive to ligand concentration, oxygen availability, and Fe2+/Fe3+ ratios [N2-F2].

In summary, the mechanistic limitations of EDTA in Fenton-based remediation are threefold: it can enhance radical generation and alter Fe2+/Fe3+ speciation, but it also introduces side reactions, pH sensitivity, and dependence on soil organic matter and ligand-metal interactions [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The result is a system that can be more reactive under controlled conditions, yet less predictable and more vulnerable to field variability [N2-F2][N3-R3].
node_outputs.N7:
Environmental limitations of EDTA in soil and groundwater

EDTA is environmentally persistent and has a complex fate in soil and groundwater. The direct evidence states that EDTA can be extremely persistent in wastewater treatment plants (WWTP) and also in natural waters, while DTPA seems more biodegradable [N1-F1]. It further says that EDTA and DTPA are generally found in the receiving waters of many industrial areas, classifying them as one of the major organic pollutants discharged into waters [N1-F1]. Although EDTA is not expected to be acutely toxic to aquatic organisms, the same source warns that it can contribute to aquatic toxicity at significantly lower concentrations than those determined by short-term toxicity tests [N1-F1]. This implies that EDTA’s ecological risk is not only from acute toxicity but also from chronic sublethal effects, including possible imbalances in body calcium and other essential or nonessential metal balances in animals and organisms [N1-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that EDTA can affect the essential and nonessential metal balance in natural waters and in aquatic organisms, even in the long term [N1-F1].

EDTA’s transformation in soil and groundwater is limited and uncertain. The evidence says that photochemical degradation of Fe(III) complexes of EDTA and DTPA is documented, but the extent to which these results can be applied to natural waters is not clear [N1-F1]. It also states that analytical methods for speciation studies at environmentally relevant concentrations are not available and that monitoring of EDTA or DTPA in sediments and solid particles has not been initiated [N1-F1]. These gaps mean that the actual transformation pathways and residence times of EDTA in the environment remain poorly characterized. The review further notes that chemical speciation, adsorption, overall degradation, and eutrophication effects are still uncertain [N1-F1]. Taken together, EDTA appears to persist in the environment, with only limited evidence for complete degradation, and the environmental fate is highly dependent on complex interactions with metals, organic matter, and water chemistry [N1-F1].

The ecological risk from EDTA and its byproducts is considerable. EDTA can mobilize heavy metals, which increases exposure to humans and aquatic organisms [N1-R3]. The same source explains that EDTA forms strong complexes with toxic heavy metals and mobilizes them, which increases exposure [N1-R3]. This mobilization is both a remediation mechanism and an ecological risk: while it can make contaminants more available for oxidation in Fenton-based systems, it can also increase bioavailability and transport of metals in the environment [N1-R3]. The evidence also mentions that several EDTA-degrading bacteria exist in nature, suggesting that biodegradation is possible but not necessarily sufficient to eliminate environmental concerns [N1-R3]. The direct review further says that EDTA can desorb heavy metals bound to sediments and prevent heavy metal sedimentation, thus increasing their cycle in water [N1-F1]. Although these metal complexes are not expected to be as bioavailable as free metal ions, the evidence still cautions that EDTA can contribute to aquatic toxicity and that chronic effects remain understudied [N1-F1]. This means that the ecological risk is not only from EDTA itself, but also from its interaction with metals and the resulting changes in metal speciation and availability.

The long-term environmental tradeoffs of mobilizing contaminants versus residual EDTA are significant. On one hand, EDTA can enhance contaminant mobilization and make metals more accessible for remediation [N1-R3]. On the other hand, residual EDTA persists in the environment and can continue to affect metal balances and aquatic organisms [N1-F1]. The evidence explicitly states that EDTA and DTPA contribute to the general chemicalization of the aquatic environment and can cause several indirect and, under extreme circumstances, direct effects [N1-F1]. It also warns that their release into natural waters should be minimized wherever possible [N1-F1]. The tradeoff is therefore a classic remediation dilemma: EDTA can improve short-term contaminant mobilization, but it may leave behind a persistent, ecologically disruptive chemical residue [N1-F1]. The review further emphasizes that estimating chronic effects and the possible imbalance of body calcium in animals and other organisms requires more study [N1-F1]. This indicates that the environmental tradeoff is not simply between removal and persistence; it is also between enhanced remediation performance and long-term ecological disruption [N1-F1].

In short, the environmental limitations of EDTA are persistence, uncertain transformation, mobilization of metals, and chronic ecological risks [N1-F1][N1-R3]. EDTA is not acutely toxic, but it can persist and contribute to toxicity at lower concentrations, and it can alter metal speciation in a way that increases exposure and ecological risk [N1-F1][N1-R3].
node_outputs.N10:
Practical and operational constraints of EDTA use

EDTA use in remediation systems faces several practical and operational constraints. One major constraint is cost. The evidence notes that hEDTA is presented as a sustainable and economically alternative to NTA, with a cost of 23 € m−3 of growth medium compared to 13 € m−3 with NTA [N5-F4]. While this comparison is in a fermentation context rather than soil remediation, it still indicates that EDTA-related alternatives can have meaningful economic implications, and the source explicitly identifies hEDTA as a cost-wise sustainable economic alternative [N5-F4]. The broader evidence also highlights that EDTA is commonly used as a low-cost and easily available additive [N2-F2], suggesting that cost is a reason for its adoption in some contexts, but not necessarily a constraint in itself. However, the practical implication is that EDTA-based systems may still be expensive relative to other alternatives when scaled up, and the need for careful cost-benefit analysis remains relevant [N5-F4].

Scalability and field implementation barriers are another concern. The evidence shows that EDTA is used in laboratory and small-scale studies, such as soil washing and phytoremediation pot experiments [N4-R1][N4-R2]. However, the literature also indicates that EDTA can create practical challenges in the field. For example, EDTA-enhanced phytoremediation of heavy metals from sludge soil was studied through pot experiments, implying that field implementation requires careful optimization [N4-R1]. The evidence also notes that the benefits of using sewage sludge over EDTA to remediate contaminated soils remain unclear and need to be assessed in terms of factors beyond soil fertility [N4-R5]. This suggests that field implementation is not trivial and that EDTA may not be the best choice for every site because its performance depends on soil fertility and other site-specific variables [N4-R5]. The broader remediation literature further notes that soil recovery from heavy metal pollution depends on the specific metals present, their speciation, and the site context [N6-R2], reinforcing the idea that EDTA is not universally scalable.

Sludge or residue generation and downstream handling are important operational constraints. The evidence states that EDTA can increase the mobility of several elements in the soil and cause plant productivity losses and nutritional imbalances [N4-R4]. This implies that EDTA can generate a more mobile soil solution, which may increase sludge or residue volume if the system is not tightly controlled. The evidence also notes that EDTA is commonly used in soil remediation, which means that residue handling is part of the practical burden rather than an incidental side effect [N2-F2]. The same source indicates that EDTA is used in soil and groundwater treatment and that Fenton-based systems are often coupled with EDTA to upgrade decontamination capacity [N2-F2]. This dual use—EDTA as a mobilizing agent and as part of Fenton chemistry—means that residue handling may involve both metal-containing sludge and EDTA-containing waste streams. The evidence further says that EDTA is one of the major organic pollutants discharged into waters [N1-F1], which underscores the downstream environmental burden of residual EDTA.

Regulatory and site-specific constraints are also significant. The evidence notes that EDTA can be classified as one of the major organic pollutants discharged into waters, and it warns that its release into natural waters should be minimized wherever possible [N1-F1]. This implies regulatory scrutiny in many jurisdictions, especially where water quality standards are stringent. The evidence also states that EDTA is commonly used in soil remediation and that its environmental fate is of concern because it has been observed at higher concentrations in some anthropogenically impacted waters than other compounds [N1-R2]. This regulatory context means that site-specific constraints are not merely technical; they are also legal and environmental. The review on alternatives explicitly identifies EDDS and hEDTA as suitable non-toxic alternatives in some contexts, which suggests that regulatory acceptance is a barrier to EDTA use in sensitive environments [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that EDTA is used in soil remediation, but the benefits of using sewage sludge over EDTA remain unclear and need to be assessed in terms of factors beyond soil fertility [N4-R5]. This indicates that regulatory and site-specific constraints are part of a broader remediation decision framework rather than a single technical limitation.

In conclusion, the practical and operational constraints of EDTA use include cost, scalability, field implementation barriers, sludge or residue generation, and regulatory and site-specific constraints [N5-F4][N4-R5][N1-F1]. While EDTA is often described as low-cost and easily available [N2-F2], its practical use is limited by the need for careful site-specific optimization, downstream residue management, and regulatory control [N4-R5][N1-F1].

Functional and contaminant-specific limitations of EDTA

EDTA’s treatment efficiency is not uniform across contaminants and soil types, and its performance is often constrained by contaminant-specific behavior, soil composition, and operating conditions. The evidence shows that EDTA is commonly used in soil remediation and that it is coupled with Fenton systems to upgrade decontamination capacity [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also indicates that the ability of reactive species in EDTA-Fenton systems has not been fully explored and its generation mechanism still remains to be unveiled [N2-F2]. This suggests that EDTA can improve remediation performance in some cases, but the mechanism is not fully understood, and its efficiency can therefore be inconsistent.

For soil contaminants, EDTA is most relevant when mobilizing heavy metals or other metal-bound pollutants. The evidence states that EDTA forms strong complexes with toxic heavy metals and mobilizes them, which increases exposure [N1-R3]. This is a major functional advantage for remediating heavy metal contamination, because it makes metals more available for subsequent treatment. However, the same source notes that several EDTA-degrading bacteria exist in nature, indicating that EDTA’s effect on metal mobilization is not permanent and may be limited by biodegradation in the field [N1-R3]. In addition, the evidence notes that EDTA can desorb heavy metals bound to sediments and prevent heavy metal sedimentation, thus increasing their cycle in water [N1-F1]. While this can improve remediation performance, it also increases the environmental persistence of EDTA and its interaction with metals [N1-F1].

The evidence also highlights that EDTA can be less effective or harmful in certain soil conditions. The Fenton reaction is affected by soil organic matter, and the review explicitly states that SOM can sometimes act in a dual way, either promoting or inhibiting the reaction, with the effects being sometimes conflicting [N3-F3]. The evidence further notes that SOM effects on Fenton reaction are reported either promoting or inhibiting and sometimes both, and that the most studied and effective parameters for evaluating SOM’s impact are initial reagents and pH [N3-F3]. In the context of EDTA-enhanced Fenton, this means that EDTA may improve reactivity under certain conditions but may also be suppressed by organic matter in other conditions. The evidence also says that pH change, H2O2 scavenging via non-productive reactions, and delivery of H2O2, Fe2+, acid, and other factors can limit the reaction [N3-R1]. This indicates that EDTA is sensitive to the soil matrix and that its efficiency depends on the presence of organic matter and pH.

The evidence further shows that EDTA is less effective or harmful in some cases because it can create nutritional imbalances and reduce plant productivity. The evidence states that the addition of EDTA led to plant productivity losses and nutritional imbalances because it increased the mobility of several elements in the soil [N4-R4]. This is a direct case where EDTA’s mobilizing effect becomes harmful rather than beneficial. The same source says that EDTA-enhanced phytoremediation was studied through pot experiments, indicating that field performance is not guaranteed and that EDTA can have adverse agronomic effects [N4-R1]. The evidence also notes that the benefits of using sewage sludge over EDTA to remediate contaminated soils remain unclear and need to be assessed in terms of factors beyond soil fertility [N4-R5]. This suggests that EDTA is not universally superior; its value depends on the specific remediation goal, the site, and the broader ecosystem.

The contaminant-specific limitations are also evident. The review on soil recovery from heavy metal pollution states that soil recovery from heavy metal pollution is possible, but the methods used depend on the specific metals present, their speciation, and the site context [N6-R2]. # Integrated assessment of environmental and functional limitations of EDTA in Fenton-based soil remediation

EDTA is a widely used chelating agent in soil remediation because it can mobilize heavy metals and improve Fenton-based oxidation. However, its use in Fenton-based soil remediation is limited by a combination of environmental persistence, mechanistic complexity, functional variability, and practical constraints. Below is an integrated assessment organized by the main categories of limitation.

## 1) Environmental limitations

### 1.1 Persistence and uncertain transformation
EDTA is environmentally persistent and can remain in soil and groundwater for long periods. The evidence states that EDTA can be extremely persistent in wastewater treatment plants and also in natural waters, while DTPA seems more biodegradable [N1-F1]. It also says that EDTA and DTPA are generally found in the receiving waters of many industrial areas and are classified as one of the major organic pollutants discharged into waters [N1-F1]. This persistence means that EDTA does not simply disappear after remediation; it can continue to accumulate in the environment.

The transformation pathways of EDTA remain uncertain. The evidence notes that photochemical degradation of Fe(III) complexes of EDTA and DTPA is documented, but the extent to which these results can be applied to natural waters is not clear [N1-F1]. It also says that analytical methods for speciation studies at environmentally relevant concentrations are not available and that monitoring of EDTA or DTPA in sediments and solid particles has not been initiated [N1-F1]. These gaps mean that the actual degradation, adsorption, and long-term fate of EDTA in the field remain poorly characterized.

### 1.2 Ecotoxicity and ecological risk
EDTA is not expected to be acutely toxic to aquatic organisms, but it can contribute to aquatic toxicity at significantly lower concentrations than those determined by short-term toxicity tests [N1-F1]. The same source warns that EDTA can affect the essential and nonessential metal balance in natural waters and in aquatic organisms, even in the long term [N1-F1]. This suggests that the ecological risk of EDTA comes not only from direct toxicity but also from chronic sublethal effects, including possible imbalances in body calcium and other metal balances [N1-F1].

EDTA can also mobilize toxic heavy metals, which increases exposure to humans and aquatic organisms. The evidence states that EDTA forms strong complexes with toxic heavy metals and mobilizes them, which increases exposure [N1-R3]. This mobilization is both a remediation mechanism and an ecological risk: while it can make metals more available for oxidation, it can also increase bioavailability and transport of metals in the environment [N1-R3]. The evidence also says that EDTA can desorb heavy metals bound to sediments and prevent heavy metal sedimentation, thus increasing their cycle in water [N1-F1]. Although these metal complexes are not expected to be as bioavailable as free metal ions, they can still contribute to aquatic toxicity and chronic ecological effects [N1-F1].

### 1.3 Long-term tradeoffs
The environmental tradeoffs of using EDTA are clear. On one hand, EDTA can enhance contaminant mobilization and make metals more accessible for remediation [N1-R3]. On the other hand, residual EDTA persists in the environment and can continue to affect metal balances and aquatic organisms [N1-F1]. The evidence explicitly states that EDTA and DTPA contribute to the general chemicalization of the aquatic environment and can cause several indirect and, under extreme circumstances, direct effects [N1-F1]. It also warns that their release into natural waters should be minimized wherever possible [N1-F1]. This means that the environmental tradeoff is not simply between removal and persistence; it is also between enhanced remediation performance and long-term ecological disruption [N1-F1].

## 2) Mechanistic limitations

### 2.1 How EDTA affects Fenton reactivity and radical generation
EDTA can improve Fenton reactivity by altering the redox behavior of Fe3+/Fe2+ and influencing radical generation. The evidence says that the complexation of EDTA with Fe3+ could enhance the Fe2+ generation reaction by H2O2 and that EDTA-chelated Fenton reaction can activate O2 via in-situ generated H2O2 and additionally added H2O2 [N2-F2]. At the same time, the literature emphasizes that Fenton systems are broader than just •OH; they generate multiple reactive oxygen species, including O2•− and possibly singlet oxygen, and that these species are produced through chain reactions involving Fe2+/Fe3+ and H2O2 [N2-F2]. EDTA therefore does not simply increase •OH yield; it can shift the overall radical configuration and the balance between different ROS species [N2-F2].

### 2.2 Limitations from soil organic matter and pH sensitivity
Soil organic matter is a major mechanistic limitation. The Fenton reaction is affected by soil organic matter, and the evidence states that SOM can sometimes act in a dual way, either promoting or inhibiting the reaction, with the effects sometimes conflicting [N3-F3]. The same source notes that the effects of SOM on Fenton reaction are reported either promoting or inhibiting and sometimes both, and that the most studied and effective parameters for evaluating SOM’s impact are initial reagents and pH [N3-F3]. In the context of EDTA-enhanced Fenton, this means that SOM can interfere with reactivity by scavenging radicals, changing the delivery of H2O2 or Fe2+/Fe3+, or altering the microenvironment in a way that suppresses efficiency [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that pH change, H2O2 scavenging via non-productive reactions, and delivery of H2O2, Fe2+, acid, and other factors can limit the reaction [N3-R1]. This implies that EDTA-based Fenton remediation is not inherently robust to organic matter and pH; rather, it depends on careful control of the operating conditions.

pH sensitivity is another critical limitation. The Fenton process requires acidification and subsequent neutralization, and the pH range is a major disadvantage of the process [N3-R3]. The evidence also says that EDTA and other iron sources were studied in the photo-Fenton process at natural pH to remove micropollutants, suggesting that pH is a critical variable for both conventional and EDTA-enhanced systems [N3-R2]. This means that EDTA can improve reactivity under optimized conditions, but it may also make the system vulnerable to pH shifts in the field, where natural variation is common [N3-R3][N3-F3].

### 2.3 Speciation effects on Fe2+/Fe3+ and radical yield
EDTA can change the redox potential of the Fe3+/Fe2+ pair, which improves the activity of iron with dissolved oxygen for producing reactive oxygen species [N2-F2]. However, this speciation effect can also create dependence on ligand-metal interactions. The evidence notes that EDTA is commonly used in chemical processes and as an additive, but it also says that the ability of reactive species in EDTA-Fenton systems has not been fully explored and its generation mechanism still remains to be unveiled [N2-F2]. In other words, EDTA can create a more favorable speciation environment for radicals, but the exact mechanism and resulting radical yield are not fully understood. The mechanistic complexity is further compounded by the fact that ligands can influence oxygen as an electron acceptor and that the ratio of Fe2+ to ligand can determine whether O2•− is rapidly converted to •OH or accumulates [N2-F2]. This indicates that EDTA may improve speciation-dependent radical yield, but only within a narrow set of conditions that are sensitive to ligand concentration, oxygen availability, and Fe2+/Fe3+ ratios [N2-F2].

## 3) Functional and contaminant-specific limitations

### 3.1 Treatment efficiency versus contaminant-specific performance
EDTA’s treatment efficiency is not uniform across contaminants and soil types. The evidence shows that EDTA is commonly used in soil remediation and that it is coupled with Fenton systems to upgrade decontamination capacity [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also indicates that the ability of reactive species in EDTA-Fenton systems has not been fully explored and its generation mechanism still remains to be unveiled [N2-F2]. This suggests that EDTA can improve remediation performance in some cases, but the mechanism is not fully understood, and its efficiency can therefore be inconsistent.

### 3.2 Limitations for different soil contaminants and soil types
EDTA is most relevant when mobilizing heavy metals or other metal-bound pollutants. The evidence states that EDTA forms strong complexes with toxic heavy metals and mobilizes them, which increases exposure [N1-R3]. This is a major functional advantage for remediating heavy metal contamination, because it makes metals more available for subsequent treatment. However, the same source notes that several EDTA-degrading bacteria exist in nature, indicating that EDTA’s effect on metal mobilization is not permanent and may be limited by biodegradation in the field [N1-R3]. In addition, the evidence notes that EDTA can desorb heavy metals bound to sediments and prevent heavy metal sedimentation, thus increasing their cycle in water [N1-F1]. While this can improve remediation performance, it also increases the environmental persistence of EDTA and its interaction with metals [N1-F1].

The evidence also highlights that EDTA can be less effective or harmful in certain soil conditions. The Fenton reaction is affected by soil organic matter, and the review explicitly states that SOM can sometimes act in a dual way, either promoting or inhibiting the reaction, with the effects sometimes conflicting [N3-F3]. The evidence further notes that SOM effects on Fenton reaction are reported either promoting or inhibiting and sometimes both, and that the most studied and effective parameters for evaluating SOM’s impact are initial reagents and pH [N3-F3]. In the context of EDTA-enhanced Fenton, this means that EDTA may improve reactivity under certain conditions but may also be suppressed by organic matter in other conditions. The evidence also says that pH change, H2O2 scavenging via non-productive reactions, and delivery of H2O2, Fe2+, acid, and other factors can limit the reaction [N3-R1]. This indicates that EDTA is sensitive to the soil matrix and that its efficiency depends on the presence of organic matter and pH.

### 3.3 Cases where EDTA is less effective or harmful
EDTA can be less effective or harmful in some cases because it can create nutritional imbalances and reduce plant productivity. The evidence states that the addition of EDTA led to plant productivity losses and nutritional imbalances because it increased the mobility of several elements in the soil [N4-R4]. This is a direct case where EDTA’s mobilizing effect becomes harmful rather than beneficial. The same source says that EDTA-enhanced phytoremediation was studied through pot experiments, indicating that field performance is not guaranteed and that EDTA can have adverse agronomic effects [N4-R1]. The evidence also notes that the benefits of using sewage sludge over EDTA to remediate contaminated soils remain unclear and need to be assessed in terms of factors beyond soil fertility [N4-R5]. This suggests that EDTA is not universally superior; its value depends on the specific remediation goal, the site, and the broader ecosystem.

## 4) Practical and operational constraints

### 4.1 Cost, scalability, and field implementation barriers
EDTA use faces practical and operational constraints, including cost and scalability. The evidence notes that hEDTA is presented as a sustainable and economically alternative to NTA, with a cost of 23 € m−3 of growth medium compared to 13 € m−3 with NTA [N5-F4]. While this comparison is in a fermentation context rather than soil remediation, it still indicates that EDTA-related alternatives can have meaningful economic implications, and the source explicitly identifies hEDTA as a cost-wise sustainable economic alternative [N5-F4]. The broader evidence also highlights that EDTA is commonly used as a low-cost and easily available additive [N2-F2], suggesting that cost is a reason for its adoption in some contexts, but not necessarily a constraint in itself. However, the practical implication is that EDTA-based systems may still be expensive relative to other alternatives when scaled up, and the need for careful cost-benefit analysis remains relevant [N5-F4].

Scalability and field implementation barriers are another concern. The evidence shows that EDTA is used in laboratory and small-scale studies, such as soil washing and phytoremediation pot experiments [N4-R1][N4-R2]. However, the literature also indicates that EDTA can create practical challenges in the field. For example, EDTA-enhanced phytoremediation of heavy metals from sludge soil was studied through pot experiments, implying that field implementation requires careful optimization [N4-R1]. The evidence also notes that the benefits of using sewage sludge over EDTA to remediate contaminated soils remain unclear and need to be assessed in terms of factors beyond soil fertility [N4-R5]. This suggests that field implementation is not trivial and that EDTA may not be the best choice for every site because its performance depends on soil fertility and other site-specific variables [N4-R5].

### 4.2 Sludge or residue generation and downstream handling
Sludge or residue generation and downstream handling are important operational constraints. The evidence states that EDTA can increase the mobility of several elements in the soil and cause plant productivity losses and nutritional imbalances [N4-R4]. This implies that EDTA can generate a more mobile soil solution, which may increase sludge or residue volume if the system is not tightly controlled. The evidence also notes that EDTA is commonly used in soil remediation, which means that residue handling is part of the practical burden rather than an incidental side effect [N2-F2]. The same source indicates that EDTA is used in soil and groundwater treatment and that Fenton-based systems are often coupled with EDTA to upgrade decontamination capacity [N2-F2]. This dual use—EDTA as a mobilizing agent and as part of Fenton chemistry—means that residue handling may involve both metal-containing sludge and EDTA-containing waste streams. The evidence further says that EDTA is one of the major organic pollutants discharged into waters [N1-F1], which underscores the downstream environmental burden of residual EDTA.

### 4.3 Regulatory and site-specific constraints
Regulatory and site-specific constraints are also significant. The evidence notes that EDTA can be classified as one of the major organic pollutants discharged into waters, and it warns that its release into natural waters should be minimized wherever possible [N1-F1]. This implies regulatory scrutiny in many jurisdictions, especially where water quality standards are stringent. The evidence also states that EDTA is commonly used in soil remediation and that its environmental fate is of concern because it has been observed at higher concentrations in some anthropogenically impacted waters than other compounds [N1-R2]. This regulatory context means that site-specific constraints are not merely technical; they are also legal and environmental. The review on alternatives explicitly identifies EDDS and hEDTA as suitable non-toxic alternatives in some contexts, which suggests that regulatory acceptance is a barrier to EDTA use in sensitive environments [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that EDTA is used in soil remediation, but the benefits of using sewage sludge over EDTA to remediate contaminated soils remain unclear and need to be assessed in terms of factors beyond soil fertility [N4-R5]. This indicates that regulatory and site-specific constraints are part of a broader remediation decision framework rather than a single technical limitation.

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Overall, EDTA is a useful but limited agent in Fenton-based soil remediation. Its advantages include the ability to mobilize heavy metals and improve Fenton reactivity through altered Fe2+/Fe3+ speciation and radical generation [N2-F2][N1-R3]. However, its limitations are substantial. Environmentally, EDTA is persistent, its transformation is uncertain, and it can mobilize toxic metals while also contributing to aquatic toxicity and chronic ecological risk [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Mechanistically, it can enhance reactivity, but it is sensitive to soil organic matter, pH, and ligand-metal interactions, and its exact radical generation mechanism remains partially unexplored [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Functionally, its performance is not uniform across contaminants and soil types, and it can be less effective or harmful in some conditions, such as when it causes nutritional imbalances and plant productivity losses [N3-F3][N4-R4]. Operationally, it faces cost, scalability, field implementation, sludge/residue, and regulatory constraints [N5-F4][N4-R5][N1-F1].

In practical terms, EDTA is not a universal solution. It is best viewed as a site-specific and context-dependent tool, with value in certain heavy-metal-contaminated soils but with clear tradeoffs when compared to alternatives such as EDDS, hEDTA, and other chelating agents [N5-F4][N6-R2]. For Fenton-based soil remediation, the environmental and functional limitations of EDTA are therefore not merely side effects; they are central to evaluating whether EDTA is the most appropriate choice for a given site.

Environmental limitations of EDTA in soil and groundwater

EDTA is environmentally persistent and has a complex fate in soil and groundwater. # Integrated assessment of environmental and functional limitations of EDTA in Fenton-based soil remediation

EDTA is a widely used chelating agent in soil remediation because it can mobilize heavy metals and improve Fenton-based oxidation. However, its use in Fenton-based soil remediation is limited by a combination of environmental persistence, mechanistic complexity, functional variability, and practical constraints. Below is an integrated assessment organized by the main categories of limitation.

## 1) Environmental limitations

### 1.1 Persistence and uncertain transformation
EDTA is environmentally persistent and can remain in soil and groundwater for long periods. The evidence states that EDTA can be extremely persistent in wastewater treatment plants and also in natural waters, while DTPA seems more biodegradable [N1-F1]. It also says that EDTA and DTPA are generally found in the receiving waters of many industrial areas and are classified as one of the major organic pollutants discharged into waters [N1-F1]. This persistence means that EDTA does not simply disappear after remediation; it can continue to accumulate in the environment.

The transformation pathways of EDTA remain uncertain. The evidence notes that photochemical degradation of Fe(III) complexes of EDTA and DTPA is documented, but the extent to which these results can be applied to natural waters is not clear [N1-F1]. It also says that analytical methods for speciation studies at environmentally relevant concentrations are not available and that monitoring of EDTA or DTPA in sediments and solid particles has not been initiated [N1-F1]. These gaps mean that the actual degradation, adsorption, and long-term fate of EDTA in the field remain poorly characterized.

### 1.2 Ecotoxicity and ecological risk
EDTA is not expected to be acutely toxic to aquatic organisms, but it can contribute to aquatic toxicity at significantly lower concentrations than those determined by short-term toxicity tests [N1-F1]. The same source warns that EDTA can affect the essential and nonessential metal balance in natural waters and in aquatic organisms, even in the long term [N1-F1]. This suggests that the ecological risk of EDTA comes not only from direct toxicity but also from chronic sublethal effects, including possible imbalances in body calcium and other metal balances [N1-F1].

EDTA can also mobilize toxic heavy metals, which increases exposure to humans and aquatic organisms. The evidence states that EDTA forms strong complexes with toxic heavy metals and mobilizes them, which increases exposure [N1-R3]. This mobilization is both a remediation mechanism and an ecological risk: while it can make metals more available for oxidation, it can also increase bioavailability and transport of metals in the environment [N1-R3]. The evidence also says that EDTA can desorb heavy metals bound to sediments and prevent heavy metal sedimentation, thus increasing their cycle in water [N1-F1]. Although these metal complexes are not expected to be as bioavailable as free metal ions, they can still contribute to aquatic toxicity and chronic ecological effects [N1-F1].

### 1.3 Long-term tradeoffs
The environmental tradeoffs of using EDTA are clear. On one hand, EDTA can enhance contaminant mobilization and make metals more accessible for remediation [N1-R3]. On the other hand, residual EDTA persists in the environment and can continue to affect metal balances and aquatic organisms [N1-F1]. The evidence explicitly states that EDTA and DTPA contribute to the general chemicalization of the aquatic environment and can cause several indirect and, under extreme circumstances, direct effects [N1-F1]. It also warns that their release into natural waters should be minimized wherever possible [N1-F1]. This means that the environmental tradeoff is not simply between removal and persistence; it is also between enhanced remediation performance and long-term ecological disruption [N1-F1].

## 2) Mechanistic limitations

### 2.1 How EDTA affects Fenton reactivity and radical generation
EDTA can improve Fenton reactivity by altering the redox behavior of Fe3+/Fe2+ and influencing radical generation. The evidence says that the complexation of EDTA with Fe3+ could enhance the Fe2+ generation reaction by H2O2 and that EDTA-chelated Fenton reaction can activate O2 via in-situ generated H2O2 and additionally added H2O2 [N2-F2]. At the same time, the literature emphasizes that Fenton systems are broader than just •OH; they generate multiple reactive oxygen species, including O2•− and possibly singlet oxygen, and that these species are produced through chain reactions involving Fe2+/Fe3+ and H2O2 [N2-F2]. EDTA therefore does not simply increase •OH yield; it can shift the overall radical configuration and the balance between different ROS species [N2-F2].

### 2.2 Limitations from soil organic matter and pH sensitivity
Soil organic matter is a major mechanistic limitation. The Fenton reaction is affected by soil organic matter, and the evidence states that SOM can sometimes act in a dual way, either promoting or inhibiting the reaction, with the effects sometimes conflicting [N3-F3]. The same source notes that the effects of SOM on Fenton reaction are reported either promoting or inhibiting and sometimes both, and that the most studied and effective parameters for evaluating SOM’s impact are initial reagents and pH [N3-F3]. In the context of EDTA-enhanced Fenton, this means that SOM can interfere with reactivity by scavenging radicals, changing the delivery of H2O2 or Fe2+/Fe3+, or altering the microenvironment in a way that suppresses efficiency [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that pH change, H2O2 scavenging via non-productive reactions, and delivery of H2O2, Fe2+, acid, and other factors can limit the reaction [N3-R1]. This implies that EDTA-based Fenton remediation is not inherently robust to organic matter and pH; rather, it depends on careful control of the operating conditions.

pH sensitivity is another critical limitation. The Fenton process requires acidification and subsequent neutralization, and the pH range is a major disadvantage of the process [N3-R3]. The evidence also says that EDTA and other iron sources were studied in the photo-Fenton process at natural pH to remove micropollutants, suggesting that pH is a critical variable for both conventional and EDTA-enhanced systems [N3-R2]. This means that EDTA can improve reactivity under optimized conditions, but it may also make the system vulnerable to pH shifts in the field, where natural variation is common [N3-R3][N3-F3].

### 2.3 Speciation effects on Fe2+/Fe3+ and radical yield
EDTA can change the redox potential of the Fe3+/Fe2+ pair, which improves the activity of iron with dissolved oxygen for producing reactive oxygen species [N2-F2]. However, this speciation effect can also create dependence on ligand-metal interactions. The evidence notes that EDTA is commonly used in chemical processes and as an additive, but it also says that the ability of reactive species in EDTA-Fenton systems has not been fully explored and its generation mechanism still remains to be unveiled [N2-F2]. In other words, EDTA can create a more favorable speciation environment for radicals, but the exact mechanism and resulting radical yield are not fully understood. The mechanistic complexity is further compounded by the fact that ligands can influence oxygen as an electron acceptor and that the ratio of Fe2+ to ligand can determine whether O2•− is rapidly converted to •OH or accumulates [N2-F2]. This indicates that EDTA may improve speciation-dependent radical yield, but only within a narrow set of conditions that are sensitive to ligand concentration, oxygen availability, and Fe2+/Fe3+ ratios [N2-F2].

## 3) Functional and contaminant-specific limitations

### 3.1 Treatment efficiency versus contaminant-specific performance
EDTA’s treatment efficiency is not uniform across contaminants and soil types. The evidence shows that EDTA is commonly used in soil remediation and that it is coupled with Fenton systems to upgrade decontamination capacity [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also indicates that the ability of reactive species in EDTA-Fenton systems has not been fully explored and its generation mechanism still remains to be unveiled [N2-F2]. This suggests that EDTA can improve remediation performance in some cases, but the mechanism is not fully understood, and its efficiency can therefore be inconsistent.

### 3.2 Limitations for different soil contaminants and soil types
EDTA is most relevant when mobilizing heavy metals or other metal-bound pollutants. The evidence states that EDTA forms strong complexes with toxic heavy metals and mobilizes them, which increases exposure [N1-R3]. This is a major functional advantage for remediating heavy metal contamination, because it makes metals more available for subsequent treatment. However, the same source notes that several EDTA-degrading bacteria exist in nature, indicating that EDTA’s effect on metal mobilization is not permanent and may be limited by biodegradation in the field [N1-R3]. In addition, the evidence notes that EDTA can desorb heavy metals bound to sediments and prevent heavy metal sedimentation, thus increasing their cycle in water [N1-F1]. While this can improve remediation performance, it also increases the environmental persistence of EDTA and its interaction with metals [N1-F1].

The evidence also highlights that EDTA can be less effective or harmful in certain soil conditions. The Fenton reaction is affected by soil organic matter, and the review explicitly states that SOM can sometimes act in a dual way, either promoting or inhibiting the reaction, with the effects sometimes conflicting [N3-F3]. The evidence also says that pH change, H2O2 scavenging via non-productive reactions, and delivery of H2O2, Fe2+, acid, and other factors can limit the reaction [N3-R1]. This indicates that EDTA is sensitive to the soil matrix and that its efficiency depends on the presence of organic matter and pH.

### 3.3 Cases where EDTA is less effective or harmful
EDTA can be less effective or harmful in some cases because it can create nutritional imbalances and reduce plant productivity. The evidence states that the addition of EDTA led to plant productivity losses and nutritional imbalances because it increased the mobility of several elements in the soil [N4-R4]. This is a direct case where EDTA’s mobilizing effect becomes harmful rather than beneficial. The same source says that EDTA-enhanced phytoremediation was studied through pot experiments, indicating that field performance is not guaranteed and that EDTA can have adverse agronomic effects [N4-R1]. The evidence also notes that the benefits of using sewage sludge over EDTA to remediate contaminated soils remain unclear and need to be assessed in terms of factors beyond soil fertility [N4-R5]. This suggests that EDTA is not universally superior; its value depends on the specific remediation goal, the site, and the broader ecosystem.

## 4) Practical and operational constraints

### 4.1 Cost, scalability, and field implementation barriers

The evidence notes that hEDTA is presented as a sustainable and economically alternative to NTA, with a cost of 23 € m−3 of growth medium compared to 13 € m−3 with NTA [N5-F4]. While this comparison is in a fermentation context rather than soil remediation, it still indicates that EDTA-related alternatives can have meaningful economic implications, and the source explicitly identifies hEDTA as a cost-wise sustainable economic alternative [N5-F4]. The broader evidence also highlights that EDTA is commonly used as a low-cost and easily available additive [N2-F2], suggesting that cost is a reason for its adoption in some contexts, but not necessarily a constraint in itself. However, the practical implication is that EDTA-based systems may still be expensive relative to other alternatives when scaled up, and the need for careful cost-benefit analysis remains relevant [N5-F4].

The evidence shows that EDTA is used in laboratory and small-scale studies, such as soil washing and phytoremediation pot experiments [N4-R1][N4-R2]. However, the literature also indicates that EDTA can create practical challenges in the field. For example, EDTA-enhanced phytoremediation of heavy metals from sludge soil was studied through pot experiments, implying that field implementation requires careful optimization [N4-R1]. The evidence also notes that the benefits of using sewage sludge over EDTA to remediate contaminated soils remain unclear and need to be assessed in terms of factors beyond soil fertility [N4-R5]. This suggests that field implementation is not trivial and that EDTA may not be the best choice for every site because its performance depends on soil fertility and other site-specific variables [N4-R5].
